planting.note: Establish from rooted stem cuttings or divisions after frost danger has passed; it spreads via self-seeding and underground stems once settled into the deep shade of a forest floor.

directions: Isoglossa woodii is an Acanthaceae shrub native to the deep leaf-litter floor of South Africa's Eastern Cape and KwaZulu-Natal afromontane and coastal forests, where amaXhosa and amaZulu communities have long gathered its tender shoot tips as a cooked wild spinach. It forms loose colonies under full forest canopy, tolerating the darkest conditions most leafy vegetables refuse, and dies back in a dramatic mass-flowering and die-off cycle in some populations before regenerating from seed or rootstock. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich soil protected from direct sun and frost, harvesting young leafy stems regularly to keep new growth tender. It suits a woodland-edge food garden in warm climates or a shaded greenhouse bed elsewhere.
sources: Eastern Cape indigenous forest ethnobotany surveys

planting.note: Plant the partially exposed woody caudex at soil level in spring as growth resumes; vines die back to the tuber each dry season and resprout from the same crown for decades.

directions: Dioscorea sylvatica forms a massive, corky-barked, above-ground caudex at forest margins and bushveld edges across South Africa and Zimbabwe, sending up slender twining shade-tolerant vines each wet season that die back completely in the dry months. The tuber is bitter and toxic-tasting raw due to saponins and alkaloids, and while traditional use includes carefully prepared medicinal and arrow-poison applications, it is not grown as a food crop like its edible relatives. Give it dappled shade at the edge of a woodland planting with sharply drained soil, and leave the exposed caudex undisturbed once established since growth is extremely slow. It is prized by succulent and caudiciform collectors as much as for any practical use.
sources: Medicinal Plants of South Africa (van Wyk & Gericke)

planting.note: Set out rooted stem cuttings after frost danger passes; stems root readily at the nodes and fill in as a groundcover within a season under forest shade.

directions: Plectranthus saccatus is a soft-wooded subshrub of the Streptocarpella group, native to the understory of South African and tropical East African afromontane forests, where it roots along fallen logs and leaf litter in deep shade. Its rounded, scalloped, aromatic leaves set off racemes of small hooded blue to violet flowers with a distinctive pouched upper lip, blooming over a long season wherever humidity stays high. It is far more shade-tolerant than the sun-loving coleus-type Plectranthus, making it a reliable filler for the darkest corners of a frost-free garden or a hanging basket on a shaded porch. Pinch stem tips to keep growth bushy and water regularly, since it wilts quickly if the soil dries out fully.
sources: African Violet Society/gesneriad-adjacent shade plant nursery catalogs

planting.note: Start seed indoors or set out rooted cuttings after frost danger passes; establishes best at the dappled, humid edge of woodland rather than in open beds.

directions: Salvia purpurea grows along the cool, misty margins of pine-oak cloud forest in the highlands of central and southern Mexico, where constant atmospheric moisture lets it thrive with less direct sun than most garden sages tolerate. It forms an upright, softly hairy shrub with triangular, scalloped leaves and spikes of rich violet-purple flowers held in whorls, blooming heaviest as days shorten in fall. Give it morning sun and afternoon shade or full dappled light with consistently moist, humus-rich soil, since the thin leaves scorch quickly in hot, dry exposure. Cut stems back by a third after the first flush to encourage a denser second bloom cycle.
sources: Betsy Clebsch, A Book of Salvias

planting.note: Transplant rooted cuttings or seedlings after all frost danger has passed; give it several seasons in sheltered part shade to reach full size.

directions: Salvia oaxacana is a large-leaved shrubby sage from the cool, humid cloud forests of Oaxaca, Mexico, grown for its huge, velvety, gray-green foliage as much as for its tall spikes of violet-blue flowers in late fall and winter. It occurs naturally beneath the broken canopy of montane forest, where fog and leaf litter keep roots cool and moist, and it scorches badly if forced into hot, dry, full sun. Site it in part shade with rich, well-drained soil and shelter from wind that can shred the oversized leaves, and expect it to need a long frost-free season to bulk up before flowering. It makes a dramatic textural anchor for a shaded tropical-style border in mild climates.
sources: Betsy Clebsch, A Book of Salvias

planting.note: Set out rooted stem cuttings after frost danger passes; establishes as a dense twiggy shrub along shaded forest-edge hedgerows within a season or two.

directions: Fuchsia microphylla is a wiry, twiggy shrub found in the pine-oak and cloud forest understory of Mexico and Central America, where it forms dense thickets along shaded banks and forest margins. Its tiny leaves and abundant small tubular red to magenta flowers, borne nearly year-round in mild climates, make it a favorite nectar source for hummingbirds despite its diminutive scale. Give it part shade with cool, humus-rich, evenly moist soil, since full sun and dry heat quickly defoliate it. Light pruning after flushes of bloom keeps growth tidy without sacrificing the fine, airy texture that distinguishes it from larger-flowered fuchsia species.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings after frost danger passes into shaded, humus-rich soil; it suckers gently to form a loose thicket under forest cover.

directions: Fuchsia encliandra is a fine-textured, airy shrub endemic to the pine-oak and cloud forest understory of central and southern Mexico, distinguished by its small leaves and tiny, narrow red flowers scattered thinly along arching branches. Unlike showier hybrid fuchsias, it reads almost fern-like in the landscape and blends easily into a naturalistic shaded planting rather than standing out as a specimen. It wants part shade, cool nights, and reliably moist but well-drained soil, since both heavy sun and drought stress cause rapid leaf drop. Light shearing after flowering flushes keeps the thicket from becoming leggy while preserving its delicate, lacy habit.
sources: Fuchsias of Mexico and Central America botanical surveys

planting.note: Divide and transplant rhizome clumps after frost danger passes into deep, moist shade; established colonies spread steadily along the forest floor.

directions: Tradescantia zanonia is an oversized, cane-forming spiderwort from the wet lowland and lower-montane forests of Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean, where it grows as a conspicuous understory herb with broad, pleated, lance-shaped leaves quite unlike the trailing houseplant spiderworts most gardeners know. Clusters of small white three-petaled flowers emerge from folded bracts along the upright canes through the warm season. It needs consistent moisture, deep shade, and warmth, declining quickly if soil dries out or nights turn cold. Use it as a bold-textured groundcover or understory accent in a humid, frost-free shade garden or large greenhouse bed.
sources: Flora of the Venezuelan Guayana (genus treatment)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in moist media and transplant after frost danger passes; forms a low spreading mat in cool, shaded, humid conditions.

directions: Peperomia galioides, known locally as golondrina, is a slender-stemmed herb of cool, high-elevation cloud forest understory from Mexico and Central America south through the Andes, where it carpets shaded banks and rock ledges with whorls of narrow, bedstraw-like leaves. It has a long history as a traditional remedy for wound healing and digestive complaints in rural Latin American communities, though it is grown in gardens chiefly as a dainty, textural shade groundcover. Give it humus-rich, consistently moist soil in full shade to deep dappled light, since it has no tolerance for direct sun or drought. Divide or take cuttings in spring to spread it along shaded path edges or terrarium plantings.
sources: Ethnobotanical surveys of Andean and Mesoamerican medicinal plants

planting.note: Plant small basal tubers shallowly after frost danger passes; stem-borne bulbils also drop and self-sow readily in the shaded litter around established plants.

directions: Begonia gracilis is a slender, cane-stemmed tuberous begonia native to moist, shaded ravines and oak-forest understory across Mexico and Guatemala, where small bulbils form along the upper leaf axils and drop to start new plants nearby. Erect stems carry pointed, toothed leaves and loose clusters of pink to red flowers through summer, dying back to a small tuber each winter in cooler climates. Grow it in part shade with rich, well-drained but moisture-retentive soil, lifting tubers before frost where winters are too cold for them to overwinter in the ground. Its self-propagating bulbils make it an easy, low-maintenance begonia to naturalize along a shaded border edge.
